title: KV cache: compaction and proactive reclaim (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This doc sketches a hybrid compaction and proactive reclaim strategy for the serving runtime's KV cache. Goal is to reduce long-term heap fragmentation, improve cache hit stability under mixed-length KV workloads, and keep tail latency predictable without heavy stop-the-world pauses.

Design goals and constraints:
- Support variable-length KV values (from a few tens of bytes to multiple KB) without catastrophic internal fragmentation.
- Keep allocation/deallocation fast on the hot path (per-request), push heavier work to background workers.
- Avoid global locks on allocation; prefer per-core arenas and lock-free freelists where feasible.
- Make compaction and reclaim bounded and incremental to preserve tail latency SLOs.
- Provide telemetry to quantify fragmentation at multiple granularities so operators can tune thresholds.

Key ideas (high level):
1) Hybrid physical layout: split memory into three logical regions per NUMA node: compact regions, sparse regions, and overflow slabs.
   - Compact regions store concatenated small KV entries densely with an indirection table; these are the primary target for compaction.
   - Sparse regions allocate medium-to-large items in page-aligned chunks with an in-place free-map to support in-situ reclamation.
   - Overflow slabs are fixed-size power-of-two buckets for very large items or for short-lived bursts; they trade a bit of waste for allocation speed.

2) Per-core allocation arenas + small object packing:
   - Each core has a hot arena for allocations <= 512 B that pulls dense blocks from the compact regions. Hot arenas use thread-local bump allocators with a small freelist to satisfy frees without touching global state.
   - Medium allocations (512 B to 16 KB) are handled by the sparse region allocator which uses per-NUMA coarse-grained locks and a compacting-aware allocation path.
   - Large allocations (>16 KB) go to overflow slabs or can be allocated via mmap-like paths depending on policy.

3) Indirection and metadata layout:
   - Logical KV handle contains a 64-bit pointer slot that is actually a versioned indirection (node id + offset + epoch). This enables moving values during compaction without invalidating handles while providing a simple compare-and-swap update path.
   - Metadata header per allocation is 16 bytes and includes length, flags (pinned, cold, relocated), and a small generation counter to help eviction heuristics.

4) Eviction: multi-layered heuristics with generational cooling:
   - Short-term working set maintained via an adaptive LRU window implemented at the arena level (small insert-capacity ring + sampling).
   - Medium-term eviction uses a generational policy: we mark items as young/aging/cold using access counters sampled asynchronously. Cold items are first candidates for in-place reclaim.
   - Long-term eviction uses scoring: score = alpha * recency_rank + beta * size_penalty + gamma * cost_to-repopulate. Parameters are tunable per-customer workload.
   - Eviction path is cooperative: request-time teams may trigger lightweight lease-on-eject marking rather than immediate frees. Background reclaimers observe lease marks and finalize reclaim when safe.

5) Proactive reclaim and incremental compaction:
   - Two background workers per NUMA node: a Reclaimer and a Compactor.
   - Reclaimer walks freelists and reclaims small isolated holes eagerly when fragmentation crosses a soft threshold. It can coalesce adjacent holes in sparse regions when both neighbors are free.
   - Compactor performs incremental relocating of hot-packed small entries from low-density segments into fresh target slabs. It uses a read-copy-update flow: write new copy, update indirection slot with CAS, then free old slot. This avoids stop-the-world but requires versioned indirection to remain consistent.
   - Compaction window size is capped by time-slice and bytes-moved per second to enforce latency SLAs. Operator-configurable budget controls how aggressive compaction is.

6) Soft vs hard thresholds and memory-pressure signals:
   - Soft threshold: when fragmentation metric (defined below) exceeds soft_threshold, the reclaimers and compactors increase activity within configured budget.
   - Hard threshold: when available contiguous space drops below hard_threshold or overall resident memory crosses a commit limit, the reclaim path escalates: immediate synchronous eviction attempts, preemption of low-priority arenas, and bounded admission control upstream.
   - Memory pressure sensors: integrate with host OOM notifications and platform-level memory metrics to trigger faster reclamation or temporary shedding of low-priority traffic.

7) NUMA and device-local considerations:
   - Memory regions are NUMA-aware. Allocations use preference policy: prefer same node local memory; when cold relocation is allowed prefer remote nodes only for overflow items.
   - Compaction avoids cross-node moves unless there is a clear benefit (e.g., high local fragmentation plus free remote capacity) to limit cross-node bandwidth and remote-access tail latency.

Telemetry and fragmentation metrics:
- region_free_ratio: fraction of free bytes per region (compact/sparse/overflow).
- avg_hole_size: mean contiguous free run length in sparse regions.
- fragmentation_index: 1 - (largest_free_chunk / total_free_bytes) (higher means more fragmented).
- bytes_moved_per_minute: compaction throughput metric.
- eviction_miss_rate: fraction of evictions that led to repopulating an item within T seconds.
- allocator_contention: average lock hold times and CAS retry rates on hot paths.
- compaction_latency_p50/p95/p99: time to relocate a single item from start-to-free.

Diagnostics and dump format:
- Lightweight binary dump per region with a small JSON manifest describing segment headers. Dump includes per-segment histogram of live object sizes, hole-size distribution, and top-N cold keys by eviction score (scrubbed for PII).
- A textual human-readable diagnostic mode for quick ops triage: shows per-arena stats, freelist lengths, and suggested operator actions (e.g., bump compaction budget, move heavy allocations to overflow).

Testing and validation plan:
- Microbenchmarks: synthetic workloads with controlled size distributions (single-size, bimodal, power-law), churn (short vs long TTL), and read/write ratios to measure fragmentation growth curves.
- End-to-end: run real trace replays from production (anonymized) for 48+ hours to measure bytes_moved_per_minute at various budgets and corresponding tail-latency impact.
- Fault injection: simulate interrupted compaction (mid-CAS failure), node kill during relocation, and verify indirection + epoch semantics keep handles valid or fail safely.
- Regression tests for admission control when hard thresholds are reached, ensuring no unbounded memory growth.

Operational controls and knobs (initial list):
- compaction_budget_bytes_per_sec (per-NUMA): throttle for background compaction.
- soft_fragmentation_threshold and hard_fragmentation_threshold: floats 0..1.
- arena_hotsize_limit: size threshold to steer allocations into different regions.
- eviction_alpha/beta/gamma: tunable weighting for eviction scoring.
- diagnostics_verbose: boolean to enable richer dumps (careful with perf).

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Indirection cost: indirection enables relocation but adds one extra memory indirection on the hot path. Is the latency cost acceptable for microsecond-sensitive workloads? Consider optional per-tenant policy to disable indirection for ultra-low-latency customers.
- Compaction granularity: compacting small items yields high degrees of freedom but higher relative metadata cost. Is a hybrid of fixed-size packing units better in practice?
- Eviction vs repopulation cost: aggressive eviction reduces resident bytes but may increase backend recompute time (model rekaf). Need to tie eviction scoring to generative cost estimates which are noisy.
- Operational complexity: more knobs increase tuning surface. Default safe presets for common workloads must be provided and validated.

Migration plan (incremental rollout):
1) Feature-flagged deployment: enable per-NUMA reclaimers + telemetry without aggressive compaction. Collect baseline fragmentation metrics.
2) Enable incremental compactor in conservative budget, monitor bytes_moved, tail latency, and eviction_miss_rate for 2 weeks.
3) Expose operator knobs in Console with a few recommended profiles (conservative, balanced, aggressive).
4) Iterate on eviction scoring weights using production replay experiments.

Summary:
This draft proposes a pragmatic middle-ground: keep alloc/free fast in the hot path with per-core arenas and bump-pointer style allocation for small objects while moving heavier reorganization work out-of-band into budgeted background workers. Versioned indirection enables safe incremental compaction and reduces the need for stop-the-world GC. Strong telemetry and sensible defaults are critical to make this usable for customers with diverse workload shapes.

Appendix: short pseudo-flows
- allocation_small(size): if size <= arena_hotsize_limit then try tlb_bump_alloc; on failure pull new dense block from compact region under per-core lock; return indirection token.
- free(handle): mark header as freed with epoch, push to local freelist; if freelist length > threshold then push to global reclamation queue.
- compactor_loop(): for segment in low_density_segments_sampled() do for each live_item in sample_window relocate_with_cas(); if cascade failures > X escalate operator alert.

Please review for major blind spots. Next steps: agree on metric definitions, pick initial default thresholds, and prototype compaction flow with the indirection CAS path.
